summary: Cole Hill: a 60-ft Aermotor from 1925, moved and raised to 80 ft in 1932 after a land dispute; privately owned, last reported standing in 2008.

facts.design: Aermotor LS-40 with a 7x7 foot cab
facts.status_note: The FFLOS entry (2008) says it is still standing but in bad shape. No newer condition report was found.

access.note: The NHLR says the tower is administered by a private owner and its lower steps have been removed. No public visit information was found.

events.note: Kane Republican report announced a steel lookout to be built on Cole Hill, with a watchman to be stationed there
Original 60-foot Aermotor tower built by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry, about half a mile from the present site
Tower watchman reporting fires in the dry season
Nine fires reported burning at once; one of the most serious blazes was along the Allegheny River near Tidioute
E.L. (Ernest) Martin named as fire tower watchman; cabin fitted to house three men in dry weather
Roof painted gray with the number X2 in yellow to help airplanes passing over the hill
Moved to present location and raised to 80 feet after a dispute with the landowners of the original site; 20 feet taller than the old tower
E.L. Martin went on duty again in the 1941 season
Women had been stationed on the tower as watchers for seven years; L.L. Dey of Torpedo named watchman
Registered on the Former Fire Lookout Sites Register
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register

evidence.supports: The tower is in Warren County, Pennsylvania
evidence.quote: Warren County, Pennsylvania

evidence.supports: The lookout was to be built on Cole Hill overlooking the Allegheny River
evidence.quote: a steel lookout tower to be built on Cole Hill overlooking the Allegheny river

evidence.supports: A 1924 report announced the tower and a watchman to be stationed there
evidence.quote: August 5, 1924

evidence.supports: A watchman was to be stationed at the tower
evidence.quote: a watchman will be stationed there to keep an ever watchful eye for the dread demon fire.

evidence.supports: The Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry built a 60-foot Aermotor in 1925, about half a mile from the present site
evidence.quote: This Aermotor LS-40 tower with 7'x7' cab was originally constructed by the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry in 1925 as a 60' tower and located on land approximately 1/2 mile from the present location.

evidence.supports: The FFLOS entry gives 1925 as the build year
evidence.quote: Built in 1925, this steel Aermotor tower is still standing, but privately owned and in bad shape.

evidence.supports: The tower was in use in the 1926 dry season with a watchman reporting fires
evidence.quote: The dry weather is keeping the tower watchman busy reporting fires.

evidence.supports: The cabin at the base was fitted with a stove so three men could stay in dry weather
evidence.quote: With installation of the stove, the cabin is now equipped so that three men can live in the shanty during the dry season.

evidence.supports: Nine fires were reported burning at once; a serious blaze was along the Allegheny River near Tidioute
evidence.quote: On Wednesday nine fires were reported burning in different places at the same time. One of the most serious blazes was along the Allegheny river, near Tidioute, Thursday.

evidence.supports: E.L. Martin was the fire tower watchman in 1928
evidence.quote: Ernest L. Martin, fire tower watchman, last Tuesday reported several forest fires caused by dry weather.

evidence.supports: E.L. Martin went on duty in the tower in 1941
evidence.quote: The Cole Hill fire tower watchman, E.L. Martin, went on duty in the fire tower here Friday.

evidence.supports: The roof was painted gray with the number X2 in yellow
evidence.quote: Mr. McKee has painted the roof of the tower gray as a back ground with the figures X2 painted in yellow with an outline of black.

evidence.supports: The paint job was to help airplanes passing over the hill
evidence.quote: The painting and figures are for the airplanes that pass over Cole Hill almost every day

evidence.supports: The new tower stood twenty feet taller than the old one
evidence.quote: The new fire tower is twenty feet higher from the ground than the old fire tower.

evidence.supports: The tower was relocated and raised to 80 feet in 1932 after a dispute with the landowners of the original site
evidence.quote: It was relocated to its present location and raised to 80 feet in 1932 after a dispute with the landowners of the original site.

evidence.supports: Women had been stationed on the tower as watchers for seven years by 1949
evidence.quote: The fire tower has had women stationed there on watch for fires for the past seven years.

evidence.supports: L.L. Dey of Torpedo was named watchman for the 1949 season
evidence.quote: The Cole Hill fire tower has been opened for the season, with L.L. Dey, of Torpedo, as the watchman.

evidence.supports: A 1949 item says the tower material was hauled in August 1926
evidence.quote: Mr. Dey was the one who hauled the fire tower material from the railroad siding at Torpedo in August, 1926.

evidence.supports: The tower is now privately owned and its lower steps have been removed
evidence.quote: The tower is now privately owned, and the lower steps have been removed.

corrections.proposed: 1925 built; 1932 relocated and raised to 80 ft
corrections.why: The NHLR's Built field gives 1932, but its description and the FFLOS entry date the original tower to 1925. The 1932 work was a move and a height increase, so 1932 is incomplete as the build record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NHLR's Built field gives 1932. Its description and the FFLOS entry give 1925 for the first tower, and a 1949 item says the tower material was hauled in August 1926. The story uses 1925 for the first tower and 1932 for the move.

notes_for_editor: Build history is well sourced by the NHLR and a long run of newspaper items on the Weebly page, which has nothing after 1959. Current condition and access are unverified; the registry entries date from 2008 and 2009. The NHLR page has a photo credited to Ron Stafford, but no image URL was captured, so none is listed. The brief's 1932 build year is a registry convention; the proposed correction adds the 1925 original.
